overview: Ramsay Health Care is one of the world's largest private hospital operators, running 71 hospitals/day-surgery centres in Australia, 34 acute hospitals plus the Elysium mental health network in the UK, and (via its 52.79%-owned, soon-to-be-demerged Ramsay Santé) acute, primary care and elderly-care facilities across France, Sweden, Norway and Denmark. Revenue is earned from private health insurers, patients (self-pay/co-pay) and government payors (the NHS, French tariffs, and Australian public contracts such as Joondalup) in exchange for surgical, medical, mental-health and day-procedure services. The business is in the process of fundamentally simplifying: shareholders vote on 24 November 2026 on an in-specie demerger of Ramsay Santé, after which Ramsay will be a pure Australia/UK hospital operator.

business_model.summary: Fee-for-service hospital operator paid per admission/procedure by a mix of private health insurers, patients and government payors; revenue is largely volume (admissions, acuity/case-mix) and indexation (tariff/PHI rate) driven rather than subscription-based, with Australia the highest-margin, highest-growth segment and Europe (Ramsay Santé) the largest by revenue but weakest by margin and growth, now being divested.

revenue_streams.name: UK (Ramsay Acute Hospitals + Elysium mental health)
Europe / Ramsay Santé (France acute/mental health, Nordics primary care & hospitals)

business_model.customer_type: B2B2C - contracts with private health insurers and government health systems (NHS, French state tariffs, Australian PHI funds, public hospital management contracts e.g. Joondalup/Noosa) that pay on behalf of individual patients; ~9,000 doctor partners refer patients into the network
business_model.geographic_mix: FY26 (pre-demerger): Australia ~36% of segment revenue, UK ~14%, Europe (France/Nordics) ~50%. Post-demerger (expected Dec 2026): Australia and UK only.

main_competitors: St John of God Health Care (Australia)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest private hospital operator in Australia (26% market share of PHI hospital benefits; leading admissions share in cardiology ~30%, orthopaedics ~30%, cancer ~25%) and a top-tier private operator in the UK; market-leading position in French acute and mental health care via Ramsay Santé (pre-demerger)

moat_factors.description: 71 Australian hospitals (44 owned properties) and 34 UK hospitals represent capital-intensive, licensed infrastructure that is slow and costly for competitors to replicate
~9,000 doctor partners in Australia build referral relationships and switching costs for both doctors and patients
26% share of PHI hospital benefits in Australia gives bargaining leverage with insurers on indexation
Consistently high patient NPS (70+) across Australia, France, Sweden and UK supports referrals and insurer/government contracting
Hospital licensing, accreditation and planning approval requirements limit new private hospital supply

weaknesses: Heavily dependent on government-controlled funding mechanisms (NHS tariffs, French CVAE/tariff indexation, Australian PHI indexation, the new Joondalup public funding model) that have recently run below cost inflation, compressing margins
High financial leverage and a lease-heavy balance sheet (~$5.7bn AASB16 lease liabilities) that is capital intensive and rate-sensitive
Acquired/non-core assets (Elysium mental health, Ramsay Santé) have materially underperformed original investment cases, resulting in a $305m UK impairment in FY25 and ongoing turnaround costs
Complex multi-country structure historically diluted management focus - being addressed via the Ramsay Santé demerger but introducing near-term execution risk

growth_drivers: Australia 2030 strategy: expanding procedural capacity (22 new theatres/rooms opened in FY26, $150m invested in development projects) and shifting mix toward higher-acuity therapeutic areas (cardiology, cancer, orthopaedics)

Portfolio simplification via the proposed Ramsay Santé demerger (shareholder vote 24 Nov 2026, targeted implementation ~9 Dec 2026), refocusing capital and management on the higher-return Australia/UK hospital business

Bolt-on M&A in Australia - completed acquisition of National Capital Private Hospital (Canberra, end-August 2026, expected EPS accretive within 12 months) and opening of Ramsay Surgical Centre Cleveland
Elysium and UK Acute turnaround plans (central cost reduction, agency labour reduction, site optimisation, fee renegotiation) improving UK region profitability off a depressed base
Potential market-share gains in Australia as competitor Healthscope works through financial distress/receivership, freeing up patients, doctors and possibly distressed hospital assets
Structural tailwinds from an ageing population and rising private health insurance utilisation/indexation in Australia

business.description: UK Acute hospital NHS volumes have been pressured by UK government budgetary restrictions, with 3QFY26 NHS activity expected to remain negative year-on-year
Elysium (UK mental health/specialist care) continues to face weak local-authority demand and reduced NHS overnight-care referrals despite an active turnaround plan
French hospital tariff indexation (+0.5% FY25, ~0% FY26) has run well below cost inflation and government subsidies have been withdrawn, driving an underlying loss in the Europe segment
The new public funding mechanism at Joondalup Health Campus reduced Australian EBIT by an estimated $37m gross (partially mitigated), with further indexation risk
Minimum wage, National Insurance and enterprise agreement increases (including a $20.5m FWC-driven provision in Australia) pressure employee costs, which represent over half of segment revenue

financial.description: Funding Group leverage was 1.83x at FY26-end (within the <2.5x covenant) but reached 2.2x at 1HFY26; $2.5bn of debt facilities were refinanced in FY26 and Ramsay Santé separately refinanced €1.75bn ahead of the demerger
Earnings are exposed to GBP, EUR, SEK, NOK and DKK translation; currency translation alone moved the balance sheet by ~$300m in FY26
AASB16 capitalised lease liabilities of ~$5.7bn add interest-rate and refinancing sensitivity on top of conventional net debt of ~$4.6bn
$16m of demerger-related costs incurred to 30 June 2026 with further costs to be detailed in the demerger booklet

regulatory.description: UK NHS tariff/indexation decisions (e.g., the 1.24% FY27 NHS indexation, backdated) and government policy on NHS outsourcing directly determine UK volumes and pricing
French government control over hospital tariffs and subsidy withdrawal (the revenue guarantee ceased from 1 January 2025) materially affects Ramsay Santé economics
A Fair Work Commission interpretation issue on a NSW nurses enterprise agreement required a $20.5m provision in FY26
The Ramsay Santé separation requires scheme approval (75% of votes cast) at the 24 November 2026 shareholder meeting plus NSW Supreme Court and regulatory sign-off

macro.description: Fiscal constraints in the UK and France are directly compressing NHS and French public hospital funding growth
High absolute debt and lease liabilities make net financing costs (FY27 Funding Group guidance $280-300m) sensitive to base rate movements, partially hedged (~60% of floating rate debt)
Hospital demand is relatively non-discretionary, but PHI membership growth, self-pay affordability and government budgets are still macro-sensitive

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Private hospital demand in Australia remains structurally supported by PHI membership and an ageing population; UK and French private/public hospital funding outlooks are constrained by government fiscal pressure, creating a two-speed industry backdrop
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-moderate - healthcare demand is largely non-discretionary, but government funding settlements, labour cost inflation and interest rates drive material swings in margin
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-high given ~$4.6bn net debt plus ~$5.7bn of capitalised lease liabilities; FY26 Funding Group interest cover was a comfortable 8.94x
key_input_costs: Clinical and nursing labour (employee benefits are the largest cost line, >50% of Australian revenue)
Agency/locum staffing costs in the UK

recent_developments.event: Announced proposal to separate Ramsay Santé from Ramsay via an in-specie distribution; 1HFY26 underlying NPAT up 8.1% and interim dividend raised 6.3% to 42.5cps
Joe O'Connor appointed Managing Director of Elysium Healthcare to drive the turnaround plan

FY26 full-year results: revenue $18.6bn (+4.2% cc), NPAT $329.2m, underlying NPAT ex non-recurring items +22.9% (cc), full-year fully franked dividend raised 13.8% to 91cps (60.3% payout ratio); Funding Group leverage improved to 1.83x
Completed acquisition of National Capital Private Hospital (Canberra) and opened Ramsay Surgical Centre Cleveland; Joondalup Private Hospital campus opened 18 February 2026 under budget by ~$14m
Ramsay Santé completed a €1.75bn refinancing ahead of the proposed demerger

NSW Supreme Court ordered the scheme meeting; demerger booklet issued; shareholder vote on the Ramsay Santé separation scheduled for 24 November 2026, with implementation targeted for 9 December 2026 (0.25 Ramsay Santé securities per Ramsay share; small holders of ≤500 shares cashed out by default)

Shares have risen roughly 57% year-to-date to the mid-$50s, touching a 52-week high near A$56 in September 2026, while sell-side consensus remains Hold/Underweight with average price targets mostly in the A$40-51 range (Citi $39, Jefferies $40.50 Hold, Canaccord $42.40 Neutral, Macquarie $33.97 Hold, Morgan Stanley $40.90 Underweight)

items.notes: Reflects higher base rates offset by lower hedging and the removal of Ramsay Santé financing costs

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Natalie Davis said FY26 showed positive momentum with a new Group leadership team in place, Australia delivering 11.2% underlying EBIT growth via activity/acuity/utilisation gains, and the UK Acute and Elysium turnarounds beginning to gain traction, while Ramsay Santé separation remains subject to shareholder and regulatory approval over the next two months (as of the August 2026 report).

bull_case: Core Australian hospital business (the largest profit contributor) is compounding double-digit underlying EBIT growth with expanding margins, supported by capacity additions, higher-acuity mix and bolt-on M&A (National Capital Private Hospital)

The Ramsay Santé demerger (vote 24 Nov 2026, implementation ~9 Dec 2026) removes a structurally challenged, low-margin European business, simplifying the group and sharpening capital allocation toward higher-return Australia/UK assets
Balance sheet has de-levered to 1.83x Funding Group leverage (within the <2.5x covenant) after a $2.5bn refinancing, supporting a growing fully franked dividend (91cps, +13.8% in FY26)
UK Acute and Elysium turnarounds are gaining traction (cost reduction, site optimisation, fee renegotiation), with room for substantial margin recovery off a depressed post-impairment base
Healthscope's financial distress in Australia could hand Ramsay additional patients, doctors and potentially distressed assets, reinforcing its market-leading position
bear_case: The stock has already re-rated sharply (+~57% YTD, trading near 52-week highs around A$54-56) while sell-side consensus remains Hold/Underweight with average targets mostly below the current price (roughly A$40-51), suggesting much of the demerger/turnaround optimism is priced in

Ramsay Santé/Europe remains structurally impaired: French tariff indexation has run near zero against ongoing cost inflation and government subsidy withdrawal, producing an underlying loss; the demerger crystallises this underperformance for continuing Ramsay shareholders rather than fixing it

UK Acute and Elysium are both exposed to NHS/local-authority budget constraints; Elysium's turnaround remains unproven with demand trends still below expectations and an active site-divestment programme
Leverage, while within covenant, sits on top of a lease-heavy balance sheet (~$5.7bn AASB16 liabilities); refinancing and rate outcomes remain a swing factor for Funding Group net financing costs

Significant execution risk from concurrent management/Board turnover (new CEO, new Group Executive team, new Elysium CEO) and a complex, multi-approval demerger process still subject to shareholder, court and regulatory sign-off
